display_title: Official Review of Paper2718 by Reviewer uB1e

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a knowledge distillation method for transformers, which enforces the student model to have similar self-attention patterns as the teacher's. The paper also proposes to use both supervised models and self-supervised models for KD.
content.main_review:
Strength: The proposed method has a good motivation. It makes sense that supervised models and self-supervised models learn different knowledge, and distillation through self-attention seems to be a valid method for transformers.

Weaknesses:
1. The paper proposes a knowledge distillation method using attentions. However, the paper does not compare with existing methods in knowledge distillation. Therefore, it is hard to justify its contribution. For example, Table 1 shows a 1.8% improvement on DeiT-Ti using DeiT-S as the teacher. What would the performance be if other KD methods are used? Two widely-used distillation methods, namely class-logit distillation and representation distillation, should be compared.

2. In the first column of Table 1, DeiT-S (SL) should be DeiT-S (SSL)? How is the accuracy of a SSL model evaluated? Under the linear probe protocol? 

3. How is the 100 epochs for early stopping determined? Is it purely based on heuristics? Since it is a very important hyper-parameter (based on Table 2), it would be better if it can be determined in a more principled manner. It would be good to see more explanations on this matter.

4. The experiments in the paper distill knowledge from a larger teacher to a smaller student. Since self-distillation has shown to be an effective strategy, would the proposed method work for self-distillation? i.e., the teacher and student model have the same size.

5. Some relevant methods in KD should be discussed:
   - Knowledge distillation meets self-supervision, ECCV 2020.
   - Contrastive Representation Distillation, ICLR 2020. 
   - SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation, ICLR 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: Despite a good motivation, the technical contribution of this paper is not well-justified. Two important weaknesses include: (1) lack of comparison with existing KD methods, and (2) heuristic design of many important hyper-parameters (early stop epoch, distillation layer, etc.). Therefore, I believe that the paper still needs major improvement.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
**Q1: Comparison against existing knowledge distillation methods**

**A1:** Thanks for your suggestion. We have added the comparison against class-logit distillation [1] and representation distillation (attention transfer [2]). The results are summaried as follows: 

| SL Teacher KD Method | SSTA KD Method | Student Acc@1 |
| -------------------- | -------------- | ------------- |
| -                    | -              | 72.2          |
| LKD                  | Head-level     | 73.4          |
| AT                   | Head-level     | 70.0          |
| Head-level           | Head-level     | 74.0          |

Since the SSL pretrained model does not contain the fully connected layer, we only conduceted the logits experiments on the SL model. "Head-level" stands for our proposed head-level distillation, "LKD" means logits distillation [1] and "AT" denotes distilling the feature attention of SL teachers to students on last 3 layers [2]. It can be seen that the SSL teacher combined with head-level knowledge of SL teacher using our method outperforms combined with SL logits/AT information. Our method achieves the best performance, compared to logits distillation [1] and attention transfer method [2].

The comparsion against these two distillation methods have been added in Table 3 of the revised version.

**Q2: In the first column of Table 1, DeiT-S (SL) should be DeiT-S (SSL)? How is the accuracy of a SSL model evaluated? Under the linear probe protocol?**

**A2:** Yes. Thank you for pointing out this typo, we will fix all typos in the revision. All the SSL models are evluated under the linear probe protocol.

**Q3: The choice of early stop epoch.** 

**A3:** We set the early stop epoch refers to the accuracy curves of DeiT-Ti with single teacher (see Fig. 4 (a)), since the red line (DeiT-Ti distilled by SSL teacher) and green line (DeiT-Ti distilled by SL teacher) are close to baseline around 200 epoch, we select the median of 1 and 200 as the early stop epoch (i.e. 100 epoch), and we also conducted the ablation of different early stop epochs as follows:  

| Model    | Early Stop Epoch | Acc@1 |
| -------- | ---------------- | ----- |
| Baseline | -                | 72.2  |
| Ours     | 50               | 73.4  |
|          | 100              | 74.0  |
|          | 150              | 73.4  |
|          | 200              | 73.7  |
|          | 250              | 72.6  |
|          | 300              | 72.2  |

The teachers are DeiT-S (SSL) with 77.0% accuracy and DeiT-S (SL) with 79.9% accuracy. Obviously, setting early stop epoch to 100 can achieve the best results. This ablation study has been added in the appendix section 1.1. 

**Q4: The results about self-distillation.**

**A4:** We have conducted the self-distillation experiment on DeiT-S, and the results are shown in the table below:

| Teacher 1    | Acc@1 | Teacher 2   | Acc@2 | Student | Acc@1 |
| ------------ | ----- | ----------- | ----- | ------- | ----- |
| -            | -     | -           | -     | DeiT-S  | 79.9  |
| DeiT-S (SSL) | 77.0  | DeiT-S (SL) | 79.9  | DeiT-S  | 81.3  |

We observe that our method achieves 1.4% accuracy gains over DeiT-S.

**Q5: Discussion about some relevant methods in KD.**

**A5:** 

1. SSKD [3] adds an SSL branch next to the supervisory branch and regards the information contained in the SSL task as additional dark knowledge. 
2. CRD [4] proposes a new contrastive-based objective for knowledge, which allows student to capture more information in the teacher's representaion of the data. Both the teacher and the student are under the same supervised training paradigm.
3. The teacher and student in SEED [5] are both under the self-supervised setting, which aims to improve the representation capacity of small models by distilling the distribution between positive and negative samples. 

The differences between our poposed method and the above three methods are summarized as:

1.  The above three works are all for CNN architectures, while the target of our method is Transformer.
2.  The above three methods all use a single teacher, and teahcer and student are under the same learning paradigm, while in our method, the teacher and student are under different learning paradigm and the two teachers also use different learning methods.

We have cited these references and added the discussion in section 2.4. 

[1] Distilling the knowledge in a neural network. arXiv preprint arXiv:1503.02531, 2015. 

[2] Paying More Attention to Attention: Improving the Performance of Convolutional Neural Networks via Attention Transfer. ICLR 2017 .

[3] Knowledge distillation meets self-supervision. ECCV 2020.

[4] Contrastive Representation Distillation. ICLR 2020.

[5] SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation. ICLR 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper adopts a self-supervised pretrained vision transformer as teaching assistant for improving the performance of student via head-level knowledge distillation. To further improve the effectiveness of knowledge distillation, a simple yet effective head selection strategy is proposed to transfer teachers’knowledge to the select critical heads in the student. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed method, including on classification, robustness and transferability.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
-1- It is interesting and novel that the SSL teaching assistant with the SL teacher can improve the student’s performance more remarkable, compared to two SL teachers. Experimental validation and the ablation studies are thorough and comprehensive.
-2- The proposed head-level knowledge distillation method is simple yet effective that it does not require any dimension alignment.
-3- The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 

Weaknesses: 
-1- Although the ablation studies (in table 2) for the proposed head selection strategy have demonstrated the superiority when compared to average head strategy, the comparison of the proposed head selection strategy and random head selection method is missing.
-2- It is more rational add the abs operation on Eq. (4) to decide the important of the head.
-3- It is not clear that why head distillation from SSL teacher and SL teacher only choose one head for each other. Please clarify it.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a novel knowledge distillation method for vision transformer, which is motivated by the observation that the different attention map information of SSL ViTs and SL ViTs. The proposed method is simple yet effective, which can significantly improve the performance of student. As such, I tend to accept the paper.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
**Q1: Comparison against the random head selection.**

**A1:** Thanks for the detailed comment, the accuracy of the random head selection method is 73.5, which is worse than our method. We have added the experimental result in the Table 2 of the revised version.

**Q2: About the sign of Eq. (4).**

**A2:** Thanks for the comment, but we can't agree with the comment. $I$ measures the importance of heads, if $I<0$, it means the currently selected head is redundant. If the abs operation is added on Eq. (4), the more redundant head will have a larger importance value, which is unreasonable.

**Q3: It is not clear that why head distillation from SSL teacher and SL teacher only choose one head for each other.** 

**A3:** As we reported in Table 2, we have tried to use the average of the attention distribution of all heads within one layer as the knowledge to transfer, but the result is not as good as choosing the most important head. Therefore, for the sake of simplicity, we adopted choosing the most important head. In addition, for some lightweight ViTs, the number of heads is relatively small (e.g. DeiT-Ti only consists of 3 heads), our selection strategy can be easily applied to these ViTs.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work is motivated by the observation that Transformers perform quite differently when they are trained with supervised learning (SL) and self-supervised learning (SSL) respectively. Authors sniffed the potential complementarity of the learned representations of the two learning paradigms and empirically propose to use the model trained with SSL as a teaching assistant to help Transformer learning better. The resulted student Transformer is analyzed w.r.t quantitative performance, shape bias, robustness, and attention area, which verifies the effectiveness of the presented method and is insightful for me.
content.main_review:
+ The joint use of supervised learning and self-supervised learning is of great importance and had drawn great interest of mine. By using the head level distillation to transmit different knowledge to the student, the method successfully find a conjunction point that SL model and SSL model could complement each other and shows great performance improvement.
+ This work locates itself well and is the first work that naturally joins the SL model and SSL model in a distillation manner as far as I know. The analysis experiment is inspiring and some of the results are surprising (e.g. SSL teacher assistant help the student pay more attention to the object body).
+ The paper is well-written and clear. The organization of the work is logical and the overall experimental design (e.g., SL and SSL difference justification, learning curve trend, student model tendency analysis) is technically reasonable.
+ The proposed method is easy to implement and the improvement is prominent (as illustrated in Tab.2).

- The explanation of Fig.4 (a) is a bit confusing for me. Does the green line and red line represent the performance curve of using SL teacher and SSL teacher alone all through 300 epochs respectively? If so, I suggest the authors add another two lines showing the performance of using SL teacher and SSL teacher from the start to the 100 early stop epoch, which may help the understanding of the usage of the proposed early stop strategy.   
- Analysis towards prediction preference is only carried on SL Teacher and SSL teacher assistant, I wonder how differently does the learned student model perform compared to its teacher and teacher assistant.
- I wonder whether the SL teacher and SSL teacher assistant could be applied on pure convolutional neural networks. I understand that the proposed method perform distillation on a head level that cannot be directly applied to CNNs, so I would appreciate it if the authors could share some insight or experimental experience on it.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I appreciate and enjoy reading this work as the paper progressively demisting the doubts that arose when I read the title of the paper. The combination of the SL model and SSL model is natural and the proposed methods are novel to me. Though I believe the difference between SL and SSL is still not fully discovered, this paper has done a good start and may inspire future research. Thus, I tend to accept this paper.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2718 by Reviewer FN8W

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents the observation that supervised and SSL-trained Vision Transformers (VIT) do not encode the exact same information. Based on this observations, the authors propose to include a distillation loss to guide the training of supervised classifiers. By distilling information from the SSL-trained network, the final classifier obtains better validation performance.
content.main_review:
The present submission shows that including information from an SSL trained network when training in a supervised fashion on ImageNet helps generalisation. To include this information, the authors propose to use a distillation loss. 
However, it has already been shown in previous work that finetuning the SSL-trained network will provide similar results. Actually they are even better than what the authors report. Indeed, while in Table 1 the DeiT-S reaches 81.4, the DINO paper reports 81.5 with finetuning. Moreover, in order to distill and obtain the 81.4 the authors use a DeiT-B teacher which is larger than the network used at initialisation in DINO (of course, also a DeiT-S). 
Because of this observation, I fail to see what are the contributions of this work. The proposed framework is an overly complicated way of baking the prior from the SSL method into the supervised training loop - and yields worse performance than finetuning. The finetuning should have been reported as a baseline as a bare minimum.

On a minor note, reporting the validation accuracy along epochs (Fig. 4) is not really informative, does not bring anything, except that it shows some accidents around epoch 50 and 100... The figure lacks a proper caption. This makes the paper look a bit unpolished.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think that this paper does not show anything really novel. The results obtained are worse that the performance reported using finetuning in previous work (even when using larger capacity as teacher).

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
**Q1: About the baseline.**

**A1:** Thanks for the comment about the baseline, but we cannot fully agree with the comment. 

1. Different from finetuning with SSL-trained parameters in DINO, we trained the compact student models from scratch. Therefore, it is unfair to compare finetuned model with ours.

2. All the SSL teachers we adopt are based on linear evaluation protocol, actually, the results based on linear evaluation protocol usually worse than finetuning protocol using the whole training data, such as DeiT-S, 77.0% vs 81.5% reported in DINO. As shown in Table 1, the accuracy of SSL teacher for DeiT-S only attains 78.2%. Therefore, it is completely unfair to compare with a finetuning model.

Therefore, for fair comparison, we should report the results under the random initialization. Obviously, our method achieves 1.8% and 1.5% accuracy improvement on DeiT-Ti and DeiT-S. Our contribution for performance is solid. 
In addition, our method is novel that we exploit adding an self-supervised transformer as a teaching assistant to complement to commonly used supervised teacher, and firstly propose a head-level knowledge distillation approach for data efficient vision transformer learning. 

**Q2: Caption about Fig 4.**

**A2:** Thanks for pointing out the unclear caption of Fig. 4. Fig. 4 aims to evaluate the effectiveness of early stop strategy. Fig. 4 (a) shows the test accuracy curves of DeiT-Ti with single SL teacher or SSL teacher during the training procedure. We can observe that both the SL teacher and SSL teacher can accelerate the convergence of the student in the early stage. However, the accuracy tends to be close to the baseline in the later stage. Fig. 4(b) demonstrates that our method can take advantage of the ability of SSL teacher to accelerate convergence in the early stage, allowing students to converge faster in the early stage while stably surpassing the baseline in the later stage. We have revised the caption in the paper.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer FN8W,

About Q1, we want to emphasize the comparison of these training paradigms again. For the sake of clarity, we list the results of DeiT-S using different training paradigms in the table below.

| pre-training   | fine-tuning                  | Acc@1                      |
| -------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| None           | all layers                   | 79.9 (baseline)             |
| None           | all layers with distillation | 81.4 ($\uparrow$ 1.5) (ours) |
| SSL-pretrained | linear probing               | 77.0 (SSTA)                 |
| SSL-pretrained | all layers                   | 81.5 (reported in DINO)     |

a. Distillation and SSL-pretraining is orthogonal, it is completely unreasonable to compare these two schemes. 

b. The SSTA we used for distillation is only obtained by SSL-pretraining without finetuning all layers, and the linear probing top-1 accuracy is only 77% (the third row in the table). Recent work MAE proposed by Kaiming He et al. [1] clearly pointed out that the results of linear probing and finetuning all layers show different trends and the results of finetuning all layers are significantly higher than the results of linear probing (See Table 1 in MAE). Therefore, we think it is totally unfair to compare the distillation results using a linear probed SSL teacher with all layers finetuned SSL-pretrained model.

[1] Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners. arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.06377, 2021.

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
The main point of my review was that the authors fail to include finetuning as a baseline in their comparison.

While the authors correctly point out that the linear evaluation systematically yields better performance, I don't see how that resolves my issue. It is quite clear that by expanding the size of the class of functions considered, provided optimization and approximation are not problematic, one should obtain better performance with full finetuning. 

The solution proposed in this paper consists in training a network to do image categorization, using an auxiliary distillation loss to make the activations of the student mimic the features from a LARGE SSL-pretrained network. The only difference I see between doing that and finetuning, is the sequence in which the operations are done. If one trained the network only with distillation for 300 epochs, then using the supervised loss for 300 epochs, it would be almost identical to doing finetuning. Actually maybe even better because the teacher is A LARGER model than the student. 

Despite the author's response, I am still not convinced by the results and lack of proper baselines. This work shows that one can achieve slightly lower numbers by performing distillation instead of finetuning. This result is not surprising, and the final performance IS LOWER - hence my rating which I intend to keep.
